info.bio:
Green Day es una banda estadounidense de punk rock, originaria de Berkeley, California. Formada en 1989, fueron uno de los impulsores de la segunda oleada del punk en los '90, cuando grabaron en 1994 Dookie, su tercer disco, con el que consiguieron un gran éxito, renovado diez años más tarde con American Idiot.

Green Day ha vendido  millones de álbumes alrededor del mundo, convirtiéndose en una de las bandas de pop punk más influyentes. Está formada por Billie Joe Armstrong (voz y guitarra)

scenes.name: Hardcore en la era del punk-pop: emocore, ska-core y post-hardcore
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Mientras las revistas anuncian la «muerte del punk», el hardcore se convierte en un movimiento que no deja pueblo sin tocar y genera subgéneros. El «emocore» (Jawbreaker, Weezer, Sunny Day Real Estate, Promise Ring, At The Drive-In, Jimmy Eat World, Seaweed); el hardcore progresivo de Washington (Nation Of Ulysses, Make-Up, Shudder To Think, Jawbox, Edsel, Lungfish, Circus Lupus, Dismemberment Plan); el «ska-core» (Operation Ivy, Rancid, Mighty Mighty Bosstones, Sublime, No Doubt); el punk-pop que llega a las listas (Green Day, Offspring, Flop, Pennywise, Pegboy, Superchunk, Queers); el garage-punk californiano (Drive Like Jehu, Rocket From The Crypt, Blink 182, Zen Guerrilla); el jazzcore (Bazooka, Iceburn); la vieja escuela (D Generation, Supersuckers, Zeke, Dropkick Murphys, Silverfish, Turbonegro) y el post-hardcore de Unwound.

podcast.title: Expulsion from 1924 Gilman Street Club
podcast.body: Following their signing with Reprise Records, Grimbey, who had regularly performed at the famous punk club 1924 Gilman Street in California, was expelled from the venue. They were no longer permitted to play there, and numerous graffiti messages against the band appeared on the streets of California, effectively condemning them even before their new album was released. "después de firmar por esta discográfica fueron expulsados del local, no pudieron volver a tocar en él, hubo un montón de pintadas en contra de la banda, en las esténas de gran California."

podcast.title: Career Revival (Circa 2000)
podcast.body: Around 2000, Green Day's career was perceived to be in decline, with a general consensus that they had exhausted their creative ideas. However, a successful tour opening for Blink 182 and the strong sales of a greatest hits album released by their label encouraged them to continue and create new music, leading to the "Cigarettes and Valentines" project. "Around 2000, Green Day was in trouble. The general consensus was that they had played out their string. They had nothing new to offer and people were tired of what they were selling. As sort of a last ditch, what the hell effort they went on tour as the opening act for Blink 182, who was really hot at the time. That tour went really, really well. A greatest hits album was released by their label and it sold really, really well."

podcast.title: Warped Tour Re-energization (2000)
podcast.body: Despite initially refusing ("never, ever play the Warped Tour"), Green Day agreed to join the 2000 Warped Tour after organizer Kevin Lyman offered them a chance to play "with no pressure," hang out with new bands, absorb their energy, and embrace their role as elder statesmen. Playing the tour re-energized the band, introduced them to a new generation of fans, and was pivotal to their career's "second act." "Look, said organizer Kevin Lehmann, here's a chance for you to play some shows with no pressure, hang with the new bands, absorb some of their energy, maybe bask in your role as the elder statesman of this community."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Career Revival Through Blink-182 Tour (2001)
podcast.body: Facing declining relevance after albums like Nimrod and Warning, Green Day's career was revitalized by a co-headlining tour with Blink-182 in 2001. This tour solidified their status as "punk rock elder statesman," captivating younger fans who primarily came to see Blink-182 and providing crucial momentum for their subsequent album. "What saved Green Day was a co-headlining tour with Blink 182 in 2001. What that road trip did was cement Green Day as some kind of punk rock elder statesman."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Green Day: From their Beginning to 2005

podcast.title: Mysterious Disappearance of Master Recordings (2003)
podcast.body: In 2003, the master recordings for Green Day's album "Cigarettes and Valentines" mysteriously disappeared from the studio, with the band unsure if they were stolen, erased, or sabotaged. While backup tapes existed, their sound quality was inferior, featuring only rough mixes, making it necessary for the band to start over. "But then one day the band went back into the studio and everything was gone. Where the master recording stolen had someone erased them, was it an accident? Was this theft? Was it sabotage? They were backup tapes but they didn't sound as good. All the mixes were rough and really the only way to salvage anything was to start again."

podcast.title: Band Ultimatum and Rehab (2011-2013)
podcast.body: In 2011, after Billy Joe Armstrong drank so excessively at a New York City gig that he woke up in a park, bandmates Mike Dirnt and Tré Cool issued an ultimatum: "We're not playing with you anymore until you get fixed." Following his public meltdown in Las Vegas on September 21, 2012, Armstrong entered rehab two days later. The future of Green Day became uncertain, with Mike sending letters stating, "if we make it through this and we get back together, we're either going to be stronger than ever or we're not going to be doing this." "Mike and Tray laid it up. We're not playing with you anymore until you get fixed."

podcast.title: I Heart Radio Festival Meltdown (2012)
podcast.body: On September 21, 2012, while performing at the I Heart Radio Festival in the MGM Grand Arena, Las Vegas, Billy Joe Armstrong had a severe public meltdown. Heavily intoxicated, he erupted in anger when a signal light indicated their set was ending during "Basket Case," screaming obscenities and smashing his guitar. This incident was a culmination of years of non-stop work, immense pressure, and Armstrong's role as a "high functioning addict" since at least 1997. "Well, Armstrong lost it, screaming obscenities at the crowd and the stage crew and smashing his guitar."

podcast.title: "Cigarettes and Valentines" Song on "24th Century Breakdown" Tour
podcast.body: Although the "Cigarettes and Valentines" album was lost, a song bearing its title, "Cigarettes and Valentines," was performed by Green Day during their "24th Century Breakdown" tour. This demonstrates that elements of the lost project were not entirely abandoned. "We're going to play a brand new song. This turned out as part of the 24th century breakdown tour. I think that brand new, this song is called, cigarettes and valentines."

podcast.title: "Dookie" Album - Original Back Cover Controversy
podcast.body: The initial back cover of the album "Dookie" featured Ernie from Sesame Street, a character which the band eventually had to remove. Although they were never formally sued by Sesame Street, as is often rumored, there was a high risk of legal action. Given that "Dookie" contained explicit lyrics and themes addressing sex, drugs, and masturbation, having Ernie on the cover could have generated enormous problems for the band and the label. The original cover was withdrawn and replaced with the current one approximately a year and a half later, after two initial editions. "la contraportada unicional del Duffy tenía a Epi de Sesamun Street... tenían mucho risco de ser demandados...tener a Epi en la contraportada podía generar enormes problemas."

podcast.title: 924 Gilman Street Alumni
podcast.body: Green Day are alumni of the all-ages punk club 924 Gilman Street in West Berkeley, California. They were welcome there during their early "indie days," including when they recorded an original song in 1992. However, due to the club's strict rule against major label bands, Green Day is no longer permitted to play there, along with other successful punk acts. "Gilman Street alumni like Green Day and the offspring and AFI and Primus and even bad religion aren't really welcome anymore."

podcast.title: Admiration for Rancid and Operation Ivy
podcast.body: Green Day members were significant fans of both Rancid and Operation Ivy, the latter being Rancid's predecessor. Billy Joe Armstrong and Mike Dirnt frequently attended Operation Ivy shows at the renowned 924 Gilman Street punk club during their youth. "This pleased Green Day to no end because everyone in the band had been big fans of Ranset as well as Operation Ivy, Ranset's immediate ancestor. As kids, Billy Joe Armstrong and Mike Durant used to go see Op Ivy all the time at the infamous 924 Gilman Street punk club."

podcast.title: Admonishing Cell Phone Usage at Gigs
podcast.body: Green Day is noted for actively confronting cell phone-obsessed fans from the stage, demanding that they remain "in the moment" and engage directly with the live performance rather than through their phone screens. This represents one of the stricter reactions artists have taken against the prevalence of mobile devices at concerts. "Groups like Green Day are always admonishing cell phone obsessed fans from the stage demanding that they be in the moment."

podcast.title: Album Theft Controversy
podcast.body: Green Day claimed their 2003 album *Cigarettes and Valentines*, comprising 20 songs, was stolen from the studio when it was nearly complete and on the verge of being mixed. This claim is met with skepticism, with many believing the band chose to scrap the material because it wasn't good enough, opting to start fresh and leading to *American Idiot*. "You can choose to believe Green Day's claims if you wish, but I remain skeptical."

podcast.title: American Idiot Movie Possibility
podcast.body: Green Day's manager has indicated that a film adaptation of the "American Idiot" album is a potential project. However, it would necessitate a highly skilled screenwriter to effectively translate its complex narrative to the screen. "If they ever try to make a movie out of this album and believe me, their manager told me it's a possibility. They're gonna have to find one heck of a screenwriter to make sense of the whole thing."

podcast.title: American Idiot Success
podcast.body: *American Idiot* became not only the most successful alt rock concept album ever but also one of the most successful concept records across all genres. Its success, with about 10 million copies sold (including associated CDs and DVDs), demonstrated to other songwriters and record labels that concept albums could be a viable and popular format. "American Idiots, which is not only the most successful alt rock concept album ever, but one of the most successful concept records ever, period."

podcast.body: Billie Joe Armstrong of Green Day is known for using various configurations of Marshall Super Lead heads and cabinets. podcast.title: Billy Joe Armstrong Drops Out of High School
podcast.body: On February 16, 1990, just one day before his 18th birthday, Billy Joe made the decision to drop out of high school to fully commit to music. He supported himself by selling newspaper subscriptions outside a local grocery store. "On February 16th, 1990, just one day before his 18th birthday, Billy Joe dropped out of high school to get into music full time."

podcast.title: Billy Joe Armstrong's "2$ Bill" Nickname
podcast.body: While in high school, Billy Joe earned extra money by selling joints for two dollars apiece, which earned him the nickname "$2 Bill." "Billy Joe earned extra money by selling joints at school for two bucks a piece, which is why everybody called him $2 Bill."

podcast.title: Billy Joe Armstrong's Alias
podcast.body: Billie Joe Armstrong, Green Day's frontman, is known to have written songs under the alias "Will Him Think." This fact, along with his ownership of Adeline Records (which released The Network's album), contributes to the widespread suspicion that Green Day is behind The Network, despite Armstrong's denials. "It is a fact that Billy Joe has written songs under the alias Will Him Think."

podcast.title: Billy Joe Armstrong's Childhood Musical Talent
podcast.body: As a child, Billy Joe was considered a musical prodigy. His father, a jazz drummer, taught him to sing show tunes. By the age of five, he performed in old age homes and children's hospitals, and at eight, he began playing the piano, although he initially preferred the guitar but was told his hands were too small by his father. "His father was a jazz drummer who taught his kid how to sing show tunes. By the time Billy Joe was five, he started singing at old age homes and children's hospitals."

podcast.title: Billy Joe Armstrong's Enduring Marriage and Family Support
podcast.body: Billy Joe Armstrong's marriage to his wife, Adrian, has lasted. Adrian, originally from Minnesota, holds a degree in sociology and works for a company that produces merchandise for punk bands. She frequently tours with Green Day, while Billy Joe's mother (affectionately called Grandma), the former waitress from Rod's Hickory Pit, looks after their children, Joey and Jacob Danger Armstrong. "Only Billy Joe's marriage to his wife, Adrian, has survived. She's originally from Minnesota and has a degree in sociology. She also works for a company that manufactures merchandise for punk band stuff like t-shirts and posters."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Green Day: From their Beginning to 2005

podcast.title: Billy Joe Armstrong's Father's Death and Family Hardship
podcast.body: Billy Joe's father passed away from cancer when Billy Joe was 10 years old. His mother, left to raise five children, worked as a waitress at Rod's Hickory Pit. A stepfather joined the family two years later, but all the children reportedly disliked him. "Billy Joe's father died of cancer when he was 10. He was just one of five kids being raised by a mother who could only find work as a waitress at a place called Rod's Hickory Pit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Billy Joe Armstrong's Vocal Cord Health Issues
podcast.body: Billy Joe Armstrong suffered from severely ulcerated vocal cords, which necessitated giving up coffee, alcohol, Mexican food, and Italian food. He has since recovered from this condition. "First of all, if you've heard some bad stuff about Billy Joe's vocal cords and how he shredded them to pieces, that story's actually true. They were very badly ulcerated."

podcast.body: The album *American Idiot* spun off into a very successful Broadway show, which occasionally starred Billy Joe Armstrong himself. "It's easily the biggest Alt Rock concept album we've seen in a long, long time, spinning off into a very successful Broadway show starring, occasionally, Billy Joe Armstrong himself."

podcast.title: Career Comeback with American Idiot
podcast.body: By the end of the 1990s, Green Day's career was perceived to be on the decline, leading their record label to release a greatest hits album and the band to tour with the ascending Blink-182 to regain interest. This period of uncertainty, followed by the unexplained loss of their *Cigarettes and Valentines* master tapes, compelled them to restart, culminating in the creation of *American Idiot*, which became one of the "great career comebacks of the last 40 years." "Green Day was all but done by the end of the 1990s and it appeared that they had played out their string."

podcast.title: Career Decline and Revitalization (Late 1990s/Early 2000s)
podcast.body: Green Day had run out of gas by the end of the 1990s and considered breaking up. Their inclusion on the Pop Disaster Tour with Blink 182 was a last-ditch effort to revitalize their career, leading to their reinvigoration and the successful "American Idiot" period. "Green Day, they'd run out of gas by the end of the 1990s and contemplated breaking up for good, but then they reinvigorated themselves with their American idiot period and continued to do well."

podcast.title: Career Rough Patch (late 90s)
podcast.body: Towards the end of the 1990s, Green Day experienced a difficult period where "nothing seemed to work for a while," reflecting a broader decline in alt-rock's dominance. "Green Day hit a rough patch where nothing seemed to work for a while."

podcast.title: Chaos and Bassist's Injury at Woodstock '94
podcast.body: During their infamous Woodstock '94 performance, the crowd completely lost control, throwing massive amounts of mud at the band, covering the stage and instruments. The band reciprocated, stopping periodically to throw mud back at the audience, and actively provoked the crowd to invade the stage, causing security to lose all control. The singer further escalated the chaos by dropping his pants and performing without them. After the concert ended, the band remained on stage, continuing to engage in mud fights with spectators and provoking them, which ultimately led to security forcefully intervening. In the ensuing pandemonium, one security guard mistakenly identified Grimbey's bassist as an attendee, assaulted him, and slammed him against part of the stage decor to quell the fight. As a result, the bassist sustained a massive contusion on his arm and lost two teeth. "uno de los deshubridad confundía al vierte en la jista de Grinde y con uno de los asistencies, al igual lo agredió y lo redujo para detener la pelea, embotrándolo contra parte del decorado del escenario."

podcast.body: Before *American Idiot*, Green Day had recorded an album titled *Cigarettes and Valentines*. However, the master tapes were mysteriously lost, leading the band to start from scratch and ultimately create *American Idiot* instead. "Legend has it that after the band mysteriously lost the master tapes to a record that was supposed to be called cigarettes and valentines, they decided to start from scratch instead of remaking that record."

podcast.body: Towards the end of the 1990s, Green Day was experiencing a difficult period, feeling creatively, musically, and physically exhausted, and were on the verge of breaking up. "At the end of the 1990s, Green Day was really having a rough time."

"And then the next time Green Day went on the road, it was with Blink 1 and 2, who were by this time selling tens of millions of records."

podcast.body: After gaining significant underground success, Grimbey decided to sign with a more professional label, which led to numerous problems within the punk community. All major record labels in the United States vied to sign them, with Warner Brothers even inviting the then-22-year-old, financially struggling band to Disneyland for a day, expenses paid, to impress them. Ultimately, Grimbey rejected the biggest multinationals but signed with Reprise Records, a significant label that was part of Warner Brothers, leading to them being branded as "sell-outs." podcast.title: Signing with a Major Label - A Risky Move

This controversial move led to the band being banned from some of their usual venues and labeled as "sell-outs" by many Bay Area punks. "He convinced Green Day that the only way forward was for them to sign with a major label. So going against the ethos of the punk culture they had grown up in, Green Day signed. That was a huge risk. podcast.body: Grimbey's performance at Woodstock '94 became one of the most historic moments in 90s music. Invited to the 25th-anniversary modern edition of the festival, they were still emerging and played a brief 30-minute set on a secondary stage. A heavy downpour turned the festival ground into deep mud. The band began playing hysterically, driving the crowd into a frenzy, leading people to throw mud at each other, and some even rolling in it. As the situation escalated into small fights, the crowd began throwing mud at the band. In response, the singer picked up a piece of mud, put it in his mouth, spat it out, and continued singing, which caused the crowd to completely lose control. "Fue un atentico chaos."

xref.title: Final Show March 1, 1994; Death April 8, 1994 – The Vacuum That Reshaped 1994's Rock Landscape
xref.body: Nirvana played their final concert in Munich on March 1, 1994 — Kurt's voice was shot, the band was exhausted, and the rest of the European tour was canceled. On March 3, he deliberately overdosed on tranquilizers in a Rome hotel room. On March 18, police were called to his Seattle house after he locked himself in a room with guns. He agreed to enter rehab after an intervention, then escaped. His body was found April 8. The news was read on air: "Nirvana lead singer Kurt Cobain shot himself to death at a Seattle home yesterday." The effect on music fans was profound and prolonged. The loss of Nirvana's central narrative created a temporary opening that Green Day, The Offspring, Blur, and Oasis each rushed to fill. "Kurt's death was extremely traumatic. And the mourning continued for months."

xref.title: Final Concert (August 6, 1996) – The Palace, Hollywood
xref.body: The Ramones played their 2263rd and final gig on August 6, 1996, at The Palace in Hollywood, planned as a celebration of their career. By the 1990s, the band was finally being recognized as pioneers by alternative artists like Pearl Jam, Green Day, and Nirvana. The farewell included dates on the Lollapalooza tour that year, performing alongside Metallica and Soundgarden. Lemmy of Motorhead attended, and Eddie Vedder joined them on stage for their last song, a cover of Dave Clark Five's "Anyway You Want It." The band members simply walked off stage without a farewell speech after the final song. "That final show was on August 6th of 1996. xref.body: The Ramones' existence was crucial for the formation and style of numerous bands that came after them, specifically cited are Green Day, Nirvana, The Offspring, and Pearl Jam.

xref.title: Influence on Rock Music
xref.body: The Ramones are credited with profoundly influencing countless rock bands over several decades, with a direct lineage tracing back to their original version for bands like Rise Against, Metallica, Blink 182, Motorhead, Green Day, Guns N' Roses, The Clash, Sex Pistols, Rancid, The Pixies, The Beastie Boys, Alice in Chains, Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, The Strokes, The Offspring, and Red Hot Chili Peppers. "virtually any rock band of the last 25 years, 35 years, and you can draw a line back into the past, and that line will inevitably lead back to the Ramones."

xref.body: Foo Fighters were among the international acts added to Edge Fest throughout the 1990s, alongside bands like Blur and Green Day. Their inclusion helped diversify the festival's lineup, though Edge Fest primarily remained a Canadian event. "International acts were added throughout the decade, including the food fighters and blur in Green Day."

xref.body: Jerry Finn, who had previously produced Green Day's "Ducky" album, produced Blink-182's "Enema of the State." xref.body: The Offspring, a band associated with the mid-90s punk revival, faced challenges around the close of the 1990s, which contributed to the broader sentiment that the punk revival had lost momentum and that the rock scene was in decline. xref.title: Mainstream Exposure via MTV
xref.body: Despite being an indie band, Rancid was propelled into the mainstream "stratosphere" due to the immense popularity created by Green Day. MTV, searching for more songs similar to Green Day's hits, discovered Rancid and their song "Salvation," giving them significant exposure. "But because of the huge vortex formed around Green Day, Ranset was sucked up into the stratosphere anyway, thanks largely to MTV. They went looking for more songs like Basket Case and Longview, and that's when they found Ranset and Salvation."

xref.body: Although the mainstream treated The Ramones as a joke for decades, they were, in fact, one of the most important bands rock and roll had ever seen. Their foundational influence is noted as essential for bands like Green Day, Nirvana, The Offspring, and Pearl Jam.

xref.body: Weezer was sometimes incorrectly associated with the Emo scene during its peak popularity, despite not being an Emo band. xref.title: Producer of Green Day's Dookie
xref.body: Rob Cavallo produced Green Day's album *Dookie*. He was instrumental in convincing the band to sign with a major label, offering them $300,000 without having ever seen them perform live, and had previously worked with The Goo Goo Dolls, while his father managed Love & Spoonful and Earth, Wind & Fire. "He convinced Green Day that the only way forward was for them to sign with a major label. He'd signed the Goo Goo dolls and his dad had once managed the love and spoonful and earth-winded fire. xref.body: The Network, despite denials from Billie Joe Armstrong, is widely suspected to be a pseudonymous project of Green Day. Evidence includes Armstrong's ownership of their label, Adeline Records, biographical lyrical references on their album Money Money 2020, visual similarities (such as "The Snew's nose" to Tré Cool's), the band's website being registered to Green Day Inc., and their single live performance opening for Green Day on October 13, 2005.
